mitigation_mechanism: Wetlands hold water through the wet season and release it slowly, so they can keep a river flowing when the rain stops. In a distributed hydrological model of the Nenjiang basin, riparian wetlands overall alleviated drought [ev_drought_hazard_wu23_2], and across most of the modelled scenarios the loss of minimum flow and the rise in drought deficit caused by removing wetlands outweighed the gains, meaning the wetlands overall supported low flow during the severe drought of 2011 [ev_drought_hazard_wu23_6].
caveats: The sign depends on the type and position of the wetland: in the same model, isolated wetlands could intensify the drought deficit to some extent, because water stored away from the channel evaporates instead of sustaining low flow [ev_drought_hazard_wu23_3]. Every unit behind this row comes from a single modelling study in temperate northeast China, and the model works by removing wetlands that already exist rather than by restoring any, so it is evidence for keeping wetlands more than for rebuilding them [ev_drought_hazard_wu23_2, ev_drought_hazard_wu23_6]. Nothing was measured in the field, no magnitude is attached to the drought relief, and no claim is made about a farm: the water arrives downstream.

mitigation_mechanism: Fire risk on peat is a function of how wet the peat is. Restoring closed-canopy forest vegetation on degraded peatland is said to reduce fire risk through increased moisture levels in both surface and below-ground fire fuels [ev_fire_hazard_mish21_3]. The damage runs the other way when the water is taken out: drainage and degradation made peatlands vulnerable to fire [ev_fire_hazard_bonn16_1], and in the tropics peat domes that were cleared, drained and replanted became vulnerable to wildfires that, once started, can burn for years [ev_wet_fire_hazard_ramsar18_1].
caveats: None of this is a measured fire outcome after restoration. The tropical claim is stated as a potential benefit, not an observation, and the intervention it describes bundles revegetation with rewetting by canal blocking, so no share of any fire reduction can be assigned to either part [ev_fire_hazard_mish21_3]. The remaining units are scene-setting passages, an introductory book chapter and a Ramsar briefing note, describing what drainage does rather than what restoration achieves [ev_fire_hazard_bonn16_1, ev_wet_fire_hazard_ramsar18_1]. No magnitude, no time to effect, and nothing on how far the protection extends beyond the rewetted peat itself. The benefit is conditional on the water table staying up: a restored peatland that dries out again is as flammable as before, and the evidence here is silent on how often that happens.

mitigation_mechanism: Reconnecting a channel to its floodplain, or restoring wetland storage, lets water leave the channel and spread: the water surface drops and the flood wave slows. Modelled removal of agricultural levees on the Lower Missouri lowered cross-sectional water-surface elevation by an average of 0.66 m and as much as 1.0 m [ev_flood_hazard_jacob15_1]. Lowering bank heights so that small storms spill (Stage 0 restoration) reduced peak flow by about 8% to 12% in the base-case project [ev_flood_hazard_feder22_2], by up to 19% as bank height was varied [ev_flood_hazard_feder22_6] and by up to 37% across the full scenario sweep [ev_flood_hazard_feder22_1], and lowered flow depth by up to 15.2, 14.6 and 12.5 cm in the 2-, 1- and 0.5-year storms [ev_flood_hazard_feder22_3]. Targeted wetland and forest revegetation in a Vermont watershed avoided up to $395,000 of flood damages, 5.3% of total baseline damages [ev_avoided_damage_value_gour20_1]. The degraded case is the mirror image: drainage and grazing on China's high-altitude peatlands increased downstream flood risk and threatened local livelihoods [ev_flood_hazard_bonn16_4], and wetland protection and restoration are presented as buffering communities and reducing wave damage and floods [ev_wet_flood_hazard_ramsar18_2].
caveats: Stage and peak are not the same thing, and this evidence separates them sharply. The same Missouri model that lowered the water surface by 0.66 m cut peak discharge by less than 0.04 to 0.13% [ev_flood_hazard_jacob15_3]; the partial reconnection actually achieved moved the modelled 2007 peak from 9588 to 9584 cubic metres per second [ev_flood_hazard_jacob15_2]; and a two-dimensional model confirmed that levee removal would have little effect in attenuating a flood of roughly 10% annual exceedance probability [ev_flood_hazard_jacob15_4]. Lower the stage, yes; attenuate the peak, barely. Position decides the sign: moving the same 1006 m restoration downstream along the channel turned a 14% decrease in peak flow into about a 1% increase [ev_flood_hazard_feder22_4]. Restoring many of the Lewis Creek reaches had no effect on property damages at all, some reaches worsened inundation upstream through backwater effects, and in some scenarios restoration substantially increased aggregate flood damages above the no-restoration baseline [ev_flood_hazard_gour20_3, ev_flood_hazard_gour20_4]. Restoring dense woody floodplain vegetation raised flood stage, a trade-off between the ecological and the flood-risk objective [ev_flood_hazard_jacob15_5]. Below a threshold storm there is nothing to attenuate: flow never left the channel during the monthly storm under any restored scenario [ev_flood_hazard_feder22_5]. And the storable share of a flood collapses as the event grows: floodplain storage reached 3.2 times a 1-day flood at the 20% exceedance discharge, but only 50% of a 1-day 0.02% exceedance flood and about 8% of a 20% exceedance flood lasting 40 days [ev_flood_hazard_jacob15_6]. Almost all of these results are hydraulic model output rather than observed floods, from temperate high-income catchments in the USA plus a modelling study in China, and the benefit is off the farm in every case.

mitigation_mechanism: The pathway runs through peat that has been drained. On the high-altitude peatlands of China, centuries of livestock grazing with drainage in recent decades led to widespread erosion, desertification and an increase of downstream flood risk, threatening local livelihoods; restoration in close collaboration with affected communities is presented as restoring ecological health to that land [ev_flood_hazard_bonn16_4]. The flood benefit claimed for restoration is the reversal of that degradation.
caveats: This row rests on a single cited case in an introductory book chapter, and it describes what degradation did rather than what restoration measured [ev_flood_hazard_bonn16_4]. There is no magnitude, no time path, no flood size at which the claim was tested, and no comparison of a restored peatland against an unrestored one. The effect is downstream of the peatland, not on any farm, and nothing here shows that rewetting a peat catchment lowers a flood peak as opposed to lowering a flood stage.

mitigation_mechanism: Restored wetland and floodplain storage intercepts water before it reaches the channel and slows what does reach it. In a basin model, riparian wetlands mainly decreased peak flow and reduced downstream flood volume, while isolated wetlands mainly decreased flood volume and only slightly mitigated peak flow [ev_flood_hazard_wu23_1], and across the scenarios wetlands mainly mitigated peak flow and flood volume [ev_flood_hazard_wu23_5]. Modelled levee removal on the Lower Missouri lowered cross-sectional water-surface elevation by an average of 0.66 m and as much as 1.0 m [ev_flood_hazard_jacob15_1]; lowering bank heights reduced peak flow by about 8% to 12% at the base case [ev_flood_hazard_feder22_2], by up to 19% as bank height varied [ev_flood_hazard_feder22_6] and by up to 37% over the whole scenario sweep [ev_flood_hazard_feder22_1], and lowered flow depth by up to 15.2, 14.6 and 12.5 cm in the 2-, 1- and 0.5-year storms [ev_flood_hazard_feder22_3]. Storage that is still empty when the big event arrives is what does the work: downstream wetlands that remain dry through normal summer rains kept a relatively large buffering capacity for large water volumes during extreme flood events [ev_flood_hazard_ahlen22_1], which is why the authors infer that adding wetland volume low in the landscape, by restoration or by creating artificial wetlands, would buffer the much larger volumes of more extreme conditions [ev_flood_hazard_ahlen22_3]. During a tropical storm, wetlands and floodplains in the Otter Creek watershed reduced flood damage by an estimated 84% to 95% [ev_wet_flood_hazard_ramsar18_1], and targeted wetland and forest revegetation avoided up to $395,000, 5.3% of total baseline damages [ev_avoided_damage_value_gour20_1]; Ramsar presents protection and restoration together as reducing wave damage and floods [ev_wet_flood_hazard_ramsar18_2].
caveats: Where the work is done decides whether flooding gets better or worse. Upstream wetlands obviously amplified downstream flood risks in the basin model, while downstream wetlands exerted strong hydrological influence and are the ones the authors say should be restored and conserved preferentially [ev_flood_hazard_wu23_4]; in a minority of the same model's scenarios, removing wetlands decreased peak flow and flood volume, meaning those wetlands were making the floods worse [ev_flood_hazard_wu23_5]. Moving an identical 1006 m restoration downstream along a channel turned a 14% decrease in peak flow into about a 1% increase [ev_flood_hazard_feder22_4]. Restoring many Lewis Creek reaches had no effect on property damages, some reaches worsened inundation upstream through backwater effects, and some scenarios substantially increased aggregate damages over the baseline [ev_flood_hazard_gour20_3, ev_flood_hazard_gour20_4]. Dense woody floodplain vegetation raised stage, a trade-off against the flood-risk objective [ev_flood_hazard_jacob15_5]. Stage relief is far more reliable than peak attenuation: the model that dropped the water surface by 0.66 m reduced peak discharge by less than 0.04 to 0.13% [ev_flood_hazard_jacob15_3], moved an observed peak from 9588 to 9584 cubic metres per second [ev_flood_hazard_jacob15_2], and showed little attenuation of a 10% annual exceedance flood in two dimensions [ev_flood_hazard_jacob15_4]. Capacity is finite and perishable: headwater wetlands filled by ordinary summer rain have less left for the extreme event [ev_flood_hazard_ahlen22_2], and floodplain storage covered 3.2 times a 1-day 20% exceedance flood but only 50% of a 1-day 0.02% exceedance flood and about 8% of a 20% exceedance flood lasting 40 days [ev_flood_hazard_jacob15_6]. Below a threshold storm nothing spills and nothing is attenuated [ev_flood_hazard_feder22_5]. Provenance is thin where it matters most: the flood results are overwhelmingly hydraulic or hydrological model output, the Swedish and Chinese studies observe or remove wetlands that already exist rather than restoring any [ev_flood_hazard_ahlen22_1, ev_flood_hazard_ahlen22_2, ev_flood_hazard_wu23_1], the Otter Creek figure is also a measurement on existing wetlands and floodplains [ev_wet_flood_hazard_ramsar18_1], and every site is temperate and high- or upper-middle-income.
